claims.text: Nanoparticles with a uniformly random elemental distribution exhibit higher melting transitions than nanoparticles with short-range elemental clustering.
Nanoparticles with a uniformly random elemental distribution exhibit sharper melting transitions than nanoparticles with short-range elemental clustering.
Local reductions in configurational entropy create regions that premelt at lower temperatures.
Ultra-rapid quenching produces a near-ideal random elemental distribution in the nanoparticles.
Slower cooling promotes short-range elemental clustering in the nanoparticles.
The proposed structural mediator is local configurational entropy and chemical heterogeneity caused by differences in atomic mixing.
High and spatially uniform configurational entropy stabilizes the entire nanoparticle lattice.
Uniform lattice stabilization produces a higher and better-defined melting transition.
Atomic clustering produces regions of reduced configurational entropy.
Clustered regions with reduced configurational entropy have lower cohesive energies.
Regions with lower cohesive energy initiate premelting.
Premelting initiated in clustered regions broadens and lowers the overall melting transition.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles are predicted to have a higher, sharper melting transition than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
Slowly cooled nanoparticles are predicted to show an earlier onset of premelting and a broader melting transition.
The predicted melting differences can be observed through DSC peaks and structural changes in X-ray diffraction.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticle sizes from 5 to 50 nm when local chemical order is changed without significant secondary effects.
Surface segregation and microstructural defects could also influence nanoparticle melting behavior.
Statistically indistinguishable melting behavior despite verified differences in local chemical order would falsify the proposed governing role of local configurational entropy.
